scopeMarkdown:
Make `rayx-signalr` a stable, complete and very fast SignalR client for Rust by closing the residual risks left by `cross-platform-support` and by measuring and optimizing its hot paths. The bar is: every supported target and transport proven end to end through Aspire, no silent failure modes, and throughput and latency at or better than the official .NET client in the same environment.

**Order of work:** (1) measurement first: micro-benchmarks, an Aspire performance harness with the official .NET client as the reference, and stateful sequence instrumentation; (2) a typed public error model (mandatory), so every later feature reports typed errors; (3) hot-path optimization under budgets (single-pass wire codec, no payload logging, robust parsers); (4) stability: a soak/chaos harness and resolution of the unreproduced stateful-resume stall; (5) authentication and negotiate bounds (access-token factory, browser Basic rejected, browser negotiate timeout, configurable connect timeout); (6) a transport abstraction with selection and fallback; (7) Long Polling; (8) Server-Sent Events and transport fallback; (9) native HTTP CONNECT proxies; (10) suspension-aware liveness for backgrounded or frozen apps; (11) the aws-lc-rs provider end to end and the Android platform verifier inside a real app; (12-14) stretch: SOCKS5, proxy auto-config and OS proxy settings; HTTP/2; HTTP/3; (15) CI, documentation and a green run.

**Audit baseline (current source, 2026-10-06, branch `feat/cross-platform-support` at `efc2ee4`):** only the WebSockets transport exists (`negotiation.rs` rejects servers without it); there is no proxy support; browser negotiate (`gloo-net` fetch in `common.rs`) has no timeout while native setup is bounded by `negotiate_http::CONNECT_TIMEOUT` (15 s, not configurable); browsers send Basic credentials only with negotiate, so a standard ASP.NET Core server cannot authenticate the WebSocket; bearer tokens are static strings with no refresh hook; the e2e binaries use the default `ring` provider, so `aws-lc-rs` is covered only by builds and unit tests; Android cells run as a bare `adb shell` binary, so the platform verifier path is only build-checked; liveness timers on suspended apps fire late and a dead transport is detected only after a further server timeout; the receive path parses each JSON message up to three times (type, then id/target, then payload) and MessagePack frames into `rmpv` values more than once, every outbound frame is re-parsed to learn its type, and every completion payload is logged at `info`; there are no benchmarks; one stateful-resume stall was seen once on the Android emulator and never reproduced (`interop-validation/hypotheses.md`).

**Product decisions taken in this plan (implementers follow them unless the user changes them):**
- The official .NET client (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Client`) is the behavioral reference (user directive 2026-10-07, requirement R16). This supersedes the original browser Basic decision: in browsers `authenticate_basic` keeps sending the credentials with negotiate and logs a warning that the WebSocket cannot carry them, as the .NET client does, instead of failing `connect`.
- Performance budgets are relative: micro-benchmarks against a `pre-optimization` baseline saved on the same machine before optimization, and end-to-end workloads against the official .NET client (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Client`) run in the same Aspire run, so results do not depend on the machine.
- Transport selection and fallback follow the official .NET client: candidates are tried in the server's `availableTransports` order, filtered by the configured transport set and the transfer format the hub protocol needs (Server-Sent Events carry text only, so never MessagePack).
- Stateful reconnect is used only with WebSockets. Implementation must verify ASP.NET Core 10's behavior for Server-Sent Events and Long Polling in S6; if the server supports stateful reconnect there, amend R5 rather than silently deviating.
- Proxies: native clients use the operating system's proxy configuration by default, as the .NET client does (environment variables on Linux, WinHTTP on Windows, CFNetwork on macOS and iOS, `ProxySelector` on Android, including PAC and SOCKS), with explicit HTTP CONNECT and SOCKS5 proxies and `without_proxy()` as overrides. Browsers always use the browser's proxy settings.
- HTTP version: native HTTP requests (negotiate, Long Polling, Server-Sent Events) prefer HTTP/2 over TLS through ALPN by default, as the .NET client does; WebSockets stay HTTP/1.1 unless HTTP/2 is configured explicitly.
- Further .NET parity decisions (user, 2026-10-07): the connect timeout defaults to 120 s; liveness durations are not validated (values that cannot work are logged); JSON payloads decode case-insensitively when the exact decode fails; `Error::server_message()` returns the server's text verbatim while `Display` stays redacted; integrated Windows authentication (NTLM/Kerberos) and transport customization hooks are mandatory; the paired RayX and RayX.GameX consumer updates happen once, at the end of the epic.

**Mandatory vs. stretch:** R1-R14 and R16 are mandatory; R13 (SOCKS5, proxy auto-config, OS proxy settings) and R14 (HTTP/2) became mandatory on 2026-10-07 because the official .NET client uses the system proxy and prefers HTTP/2 by default. R15 (HTTP/3) is a stretch goal ("if possible"): it runs after every mandatory sprint except CI/documentation, so CI and docs cover whatever was delivered. Each stretch sprint starts with a time-boxed feasibility task. A stretch criterion may be dropped only through `amend --specification` that records concrete evidence (missing server support, unavailable platform API, no maintained and audited dependency, or no reproducible test environment) **after the user confirms**; dropping one lowers the affected final-check minimum counts in the same amendment, and every criterion that was met stays. Stretch features are additive and opt-in, so the default behavior of a mandatory feature never depends on them.

**Typed error model (mandatory):** the public API returns one `rayx_signalr::Error` instead of `String`. This is a deliberate breaking change: the crate moves to its next major version, and the README gets a migration section.

**Out of scope:** WPAD auto-discovery performed by the crate itself (it is honored only where the OS resolver performs it under R13.C3); an iOS app-hosted (XCTest) harness (the iOS platform verifier needs no app-side initialization and keeps simulator-binary proof); browser control of HTTP versions or proxies (browsers choose them); Azure SignalR Service-specific features beyond negotiate redirects; RayX-side integration.

**Environment prerequisites:** everything from `cross-platform-support` (.NET SDK 10, Aspire CLI 13.5.3, Rust 1.92, Node 24 with pnpm and the Playwright browsers, Android SDK with an NDK, `cargo-ndk` 4.1.2 and a running x86_64 emulator); plus JDK 17 and the Gradle wrapper for the Android test app, and `cargo bench` (Criterion). HTTP/3 cells need a Kestrel HTTP/3 host (Windows 11 or Linux with `libmsquic`; macOS is not supported by Kestrel). OS-proxy cells on Windows and macOS run only on ephemeral CI runners. iOS cells run only on macOS (CI). Integrated Windows authentication cells run on Windows hosts (the test service's Negotiate authentication uses the current Windows account).
constraintsMarkdown:
- Current source and tests are authoritative; preserve public names and semantics except where a criterion explicitly owns a change (the browser Basic rejection and the R16 parity changes are the planned behavior breaks).
- The official .NET client (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Client` with `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Connections.Client`, the test service's ASP.NET Core version) is the behavioral reference (user directive, 2026-10-07: "100% full compatibility with the official .NET client"): where this client's observable behavior differs, R16 owns the change to the .NET behavior, documented and tested like any behavior change; Rust-idiomatic API shapes are kept where the observable behavior matches.
- Preserve the `client-runtime` and `interop-validation` rules: JSON handshake even for MessagePack; application-defined Serde names; cumulative Ack and nonzero Sequence; the ordinary/stateful split (never reuse a logical token in ordinary mode; never renegotiate or re-handshake during stateful resume; never send a WebSocket Close to end a resumable stateful transport); generation-checked reconnect completion; distinct lifecycle states on both targets.
- Never rely on rustls' process-default `CryptoProvider`; secure endpoints never fall back to plaintext or an accept-all verifier, also behind proxies.
- Never log, embed in errors, or put in URLs anything secret beyond what the protocol requires (`access_token` in browser query strings): redact bearer tokens, proxy credentials and `Authorization` values; never log message payloads above `trace`.
- Fault injection, chaos and suspension controls stay test-only (the .NET test service, the fixture crate, the e2e/perf/Android harness crates, `#[cfg(test)]` code).
- Avoid holding native locks or WASM `RefCell` borrows across `.await` points or user callbacks.
- Service-dependent proof runs only through the Aspire end-to-end project with dynamic ports and the 60-second default cell bound (scenarios may declare a longer catalog bound); no scripts, no fixed ports, no hand-started services.
- Every behavior change gets its own new, separately selectable test group; sprint checks select exactly those groups.
- From S2 on, every error a criterion describes is a variant of the typed error model (for example a timeout is `ErrorKind::Timeout`); tests assert the kind and structured fields, and assert message text only where a criterion requires message content.
- Tests never change the developer machine's network or proxy settings: OS-proxy cells that change system settings run only on emulators or on ephemeral CI runners that opt in (`RAYX_SIGNALR_E2E_ALLOW_SYSTEM_CHANGES=1`), and restore the setting afterwards.
- Follow the repository layout current at implementation time. Paths here follow the `chore/cleanup` restructuring (2026-10-06): .NET sources live under `dotnet/<Project>/src/`, the test service is `dotnet/RayX.SignalR.TestService`, new projects (`RayX.SignalR.PerfReference`, `RayX.SignalR.TestProxy`) use the same layout and join `RayX.SignalR.slnx`, and user documentation lives in `docs/` chapters (limitations, the former `FORK.md` residual risks, in `docs/12-limitations.md`). If the layout differs when implementation starts, correct the paths through `amend` before dependent work.

requirements.title: Performance measurement
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Measure the client before changing it, on the same hot paths and workloads the optimization budgets use.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: Criterion micro-benchmarks in `benches/hot_paths.rs` (`cargo bench --bench hot_paths --features messagepack,bench-internals`) cover, for JSON and MessagePack: inbound Invocation, Completion (with and without result), StreamItem and Ping decoding plus dispatch through the action storage; outbound invocation encoding with framing; JSON record splitting and MessagePack varint framing of multi-message frames; payload sizes 32 B, 1 KiB and 64 KiB. Benchmark ids are stable (`hot_paths/<direction>/<protocol>/<message>/<size>`) so a named Criterion baseline can be compared later.

An Aspire `Performance` test category runs identical workloads with a release build of the Rust native client (`tests/perf`, `test = false`) and with the official .NET client (`dotnet/RayX.SignalR.PerfReference`, `Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Client` plus its MessagePack protocol, same ASP.NET Core version as the test service) against the same test service in one run: `invoke-latency` (2,000 sequential invocations; p50, p99, max), `stream-throughput` (100,000 server-stream items), `send-throughput` (50,000 client-to-server sends acknowledged by a final invocation) and `fan-in` (8 concurrent clients each invoking 1,000 times; aggregate throughput), for JSON and MessagePack. Before its timed window every workload runs the same operation untimed on the measured connection(s), identically for both clients, for at least 2 s at `full` scale (0.2 s at `quick`, where every count below is a tenth): at least 200 invocations for `invoke-latency`, whole warm-up streams of 10,000 items for `stream-throughput`, sends confirmed by a `SinkCount` invocation for `send-throughput` (the final count includes them), and invocations on every client for `fan-in`; the .NET client keeps its default tiered compilation. Each workload result (client, protocol, workload, metrics including the warm-up size, environment, build profile) is written to `artifacts-temp/perf/<run>.json`; workloads and iteration scale are selectable through `RAYX_SIGNALR_PERF_WORKLOADS` and `RAYX_SIGNALR_PERF_SCALE` (`quick` for smoke checks, `full` for budgets).

requirements.title: Hot-path performance
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Make the per-message path cheaper on both targets without changing wire behavior.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: Inbound frames are decoded in one pass per message on both targets and for both protocols: one envelope decode yields the message type, invocation id or target, and the undecoded payload (a borrowed JSON raw value or a MessagePack byte range), and the payload is deserialized once into the awaited type; action storage dispatches on the decoded id or target without parsing again. Outbound messages carry their type from construction, so nothing is re-parsed to classify or track them. New frame-level `wire_codec_` tests cover every message type, both protocols, multi-message frames, unknown message types and malformed input (errors, never panics), and the existing golden frame tests stay unchanged.

Message payloads, arguments and results are never logged above `trace` on either target, and nothing logged at `info` or above contains them. A `log_policy_` test with a capturing logger sends a completion whose result contains a marker string and asserts the marker appears in no record at `debug` or above.

Against the Criterion baseline `pre-optimization` saved on the same machine before any hot-path change, inbound StreamItem and Completion decode-plus-dispatch are at least 1.5x faster for JSON and for MessagePack at 32 B and 1 KiB payloads, outbound invocation encoding is at least 1.2x faster, and no benchmark id regresses by more than 5 %. Verified by a `MicroBenchmarkBudget` test that reads Criterion's change estimates.

In one Aspire run with `RAYX_SIGNALR_PERF_SCALE=full`, the release Rust client meets these budgets against the official .NET client for JSON and MessagePack: `invoke-latency` p50 and p99 at most 1.10x of the .NET client, `stream-throughput`, `send-throughput` and `fan-in` throughput at least 0.95x of it. Verified by a `ReferenceClientBudget` test over the run's results.

Native sends complete once the transport accepts the message, as the official .NET client's `SendAsync` completes once the message is in the transport's pipe: the caller waits only for room in the bounded outbound queue and, with stateful reconnect, in the replay buffer, and tracks the frame for replay and queues it under the replay buffer's lock, so stateful sequence order equals queue order. The writer task writes each queued frame together with the frames queued behind it as one WebSocket message (up to 64 KiB), as the official transports send what their pipe holds. Errors that exist before acceptance (not connected, paused, a message larger than the replay buffer, a stale transport) still fail the call. Unit group `outbound_writer_`.

requirements.title: Robustness and stability
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: No panics on network input, observable stateful sequencing, and long-running proof under chaos.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: Property tests (`proptest`, test group `robustness_`) feed arbitrary, truncated, oversized and type-confused input to JSON record splitting, MessagePack varint framing, the envelope decoders of R2.C1, handshake parsing, negotiate response parsing (the Long Polling and Server-Sent Events parsers join this group under R6.C1 and R7.C1): none panics, all return errors. The protocol, transport and negotiation modules deny `clippy::unwrap_used`, `clippy::expect_used`, `clippy::panic` and `clippy::indexing_slicing` outside tests, with no `allow` except on a documented invariant.

At `debug` level both targets log stateful sequencing without payloads: each tracked outgoing sequence id, each received trackable id with its accept/duplicate decision, each Ack sent and received, each Sequence message, and the resend range of every resume, tagged with the connection generation. Test group `sequence_trace_` asserts the records for a scripted resume.

A `soak-chaos` scenario runs mixed concurrent traffic (invocations with results, fire-and-forget sends, server streams, server-to-client callbacks and client results) for `RAYX_SIGNALR_SOAK_SECONDS` (default 120 in sprint checks, 900 in the nightly CI job) while a test-only service control aborts transports at random 0.5-5 s intervals, against an ordinary and a stateful hub. It asserts: stateful mode loses and duplicates nothing (every invocation completes once with its result, streams arrive complete and in order); ordinary mode completes or fails every pending call (never hangs) and recovers; after `disconnect` no client task or socket remains (native: the runtime's alive-task count returns to its pre-connect value). Runs on native, Chromium and Android for JSON and MessagePack; the catalog bound is the soak duration plus 60 s.

A `stateful-resume-stress` scenario performs 500 server-side transport aborts (100 on each of five fresh stateful connections), each immediately followed by an invocation and a short server stream, with the sequence instrumentation of R3.C2 enabled; it passes on native, Chromium and Android for JSON and MessagePack. If it reproduces the 2026-10-06 stall, the root cause is fixed and covered by a regression test in the same sprint; either way `interop-validation/hypotheses.md` and the limitations chapter (`docs/12-limitations.md`) are updated (hypothesis retired with this evidence, or replaced by the confirmed cause and fix).

requirements.title: Authentication and connection-setup bounds
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Refreshable tokens, no silently broken browser authentication, and bounded setup on every target.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: `ConnectionConfiguration::with_access_token_factory(f)` on both targets accepts an async function returning `Result<String, String>`; it is called before every negotiate (initial connect, ordinary reconnect, resume renegotiation of an ended stateful connection) and again whenever a native WebSocket is opened (including every stateful resume), as the .NET client's `AccessTokenProvider` is, and Long Polling and Server-Sent Events requests answered with 401 retry once with a fresh token; the token is sent as Bearer (native `Authorization` header on negotiate and the WebSocket upgrade; browsers `Authorization` on negotiate and `access_token` on the transport), except where a negotiate redirect supplies its own access token. A factory error fails that attempt with the factory's message (redacted of anything token-shaped). Configuring a factory together with `authenticate_basic` or `authenticate_bearer` fails `connect` before I/O. Unit group `access_token_factory_`; e2e scenario `token-factory` (the service accepts only tokens issued by a test endpoint and rejects reuse after `/e2e/rotate-token`, proving a reconnect fetched a fresh token, and counting the factory calls of one connect) on all targets.

In browsers `authenticate_basic` behaves as in the .NET client (user decision 2026-10-07, superseding the planned rejection): the Basic credentials are sent with negotiate, the WebSocket cannot carry them, and `connect` logs a warning that names Bearer tokens or `with_access_token_factory` for authenticating the transport; it never fails because of it. Native behavior is unchanged. Unit group `browser_basic_` (the warning decision tested natively through a shared function and the capturing logger) and the existing `authentication` scenario on Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.

`with_connect_timeout(d)` (default 120 s, the official .NET client's negotiate bound (user decision 2026-10-07); as every liveness duration since R16.C30, a zero value is accepted and logged, not rejected) bounds negotiate requests and transport setup on both targets; browsers abort the negotiate `fetch` with an `AbortController`. A service endpoint that accepts the request and never responds makes `connect` fail with a timeout error naming the bound within the bound plus 2 s, and the error never contains the URL or token. E2e scenario `negotiate-timeout` (2 s bound) on all targets; unit group `connect_timeout_` (default, zero logged, bounded native negotiate and WebSocket upgrade).

requirements.title: Transport abstraction and selection
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Separate the connection lifecycle from the WebSocket so further transports plug in, and select transports like the official clients.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: `with_transports(Transports)` (a set of `WebSockets`, `ServerSentEvents`, `LongPolling`; default all) on both targets. Negotiation tries the transports in the server's `availableTransports` order, as the .NET client does, keeping those in the configured set that offer the transfer format the hub protocol needs (Server-Sent Events: text only, so never for MessagePack); if starting it fails before the handshake completes, the next candidate is tried with a fresh negotiate, and when all fail the error lists each transport's failure. `skip_negotiation()` requires WebSockets alone in the set and stateful reconnect requires WebSockets (otherwise `connect` fails before I/O). Unit group `transport_selection_` covers every combination of offered transports, transfer formats, protocols and configured sets.

The WebSockets transport behind the new abstraction keeps every existing behavior: the full end-to-end catalog passes over WebSockets on native and Chromium for JSON and MessagePack. (Whole-catalog scope is justified because the connection loop every scenario uses is restructured.)

The scenario catalog gains a transport dimension: `RAYX_SIGNALR_E2E_TRANSPORTS` (`websockets` default, `long-polling`, `server-sent-events`, `all`; an empty or unknown value fails selection) yields cells for the transport-baseline scenarios of R6.C2 on every selected transport and for all other scenarios only when `websockets` is selected, never pairs Server-Sent Events with MessagePack, names non-WebSocket cells with a transport suffix (`invoke (JSON, Long Polling)`), passes the transport to native, mobile and browser runners, and keeps catalog consistency with `e2e --list` and `playwright test --list`. New `TransportCatalog` tests cover selection, cell generation and naming.

requirements.title: Long Polling transport
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: A complete Long Polling transport on both targets.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: Long Polling on both targets: the receive loop issues `GET <url>?id=<token>` requests one at a time (the server holds each up to its poll timeout; 204 ends the connection; 200 delivers zero or more frames; any other status or a network error drops the transport); sends are ordered `POST` requests (one in flight, queued in order, honoring backpressure); `DELETE` ends the connection on local close. Text and binary transfer formats work, so JSON and MessagePack both run. The handshake, pause/resume, ordinary reconnect and the access-token factory behave as over WebSockets; Long Polling has inherent keep-alive, so, as in the .NET client and ASP.NET Core, the client sends no keep-alive Pings and runs no server timeout over it (an idle Long Polling client never drops spuriously); every request is bounded by the poll timeout plus `connect_timeout`. Unit group `long_polling_` (request sequencing, status handling, ordering, cancellation on close) and the `robustness_` parsers.

The transport baseline (the catalog scenarios marked transport-independent: connect-negotiate, authentication, invoke, send, server-stream, callbacks, concurrency-and-clones, large-payload, server-close, reconnect-exhaustion, ordinary-reconnect, keepalive-idle, server-timeout, pause-resume, token-factory; `keepalive-idle` and `server-timeout` do not apply to Long Polling's inherent keep-alive and instead assert that an idle Long Polling client stays connected for 45 s) passes over Long Polling for JSON and MessagePack on native, Chromium, Firefox, WebKit and Android, and on iOS in CI.

requirements.title: Server-Sent Events transport and fallback
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: A complete Server-Sent Events transport and proven fallback between transports.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: Server-Sent Events on both targets: native reads a streaming `GET` (`Accept: text/event-stream`) with a spec-conformant event parser (multi-line `data:`, comments as keep-alive, CRLF/LF/CR line endings, events split across reads); browsers use `EventSource` (the token travels as `access_token` because `EventSource` cannot set headers); sends are ordered `POST` requests as for Long Polling. JSON only: an explicit Server-Sent-Events-only configuration with MessagePack fails `connect` before I/O. Handshake, liveness, pause/resume, ordinary reconnect and the token factory behave as over WebSockets. Unit group `server_sent_events_` and the `robustness_` parser cases.
The transport baseline of R6.C2 passes over Server-Sent Events for JSON on native, Chromium, Firefox, WebKit and Android, and on iOS in CI.

Fallback is proven end to end: against hubs restricted server-side to Long Polling (`/test-longpolling`) and to Server-Sent Events plus Long Polling (`/test-no-websockets`), a client with the default transport set connects with the expected transport (reported by `TransportDetails`) for each protocol, and a client restricted to WebSockets fails with an error naming the unavailable transport. Scenario `transport-fallback` on native, Chromium and Android.

requirements.title: Native HTTP proxies
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Connect through HTTP CONNECT proxies on native targets.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: Native-only `with_proxy(url)` (`http://[user:password@]host:port`), `with_system_proxy()` (reads `HTTPS_PROXY`/`HTTP_PROXY`/`ALL_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY` in upper or lower case at `connect`; `NO_PROXY` supports host names, domain suffixes, IP addresses, CIDR ranges, ports and `*`) and `without_proxy()`; the default is the system proxy resolution (`with_system_proxy()`, which R13.C3 extends with the operating system's own proxy settings), as the .NET client's default proxy is. Every native connection (negotiate, WebSocket, Long Polling, Server-Sent Events) to a proxied endpoint opens an HTTP CONNECT tunnel (Basic `Proxy-Authorization` when credentials are configured), then runs TLS with the connection's rustls configuration inside the tunnel for secure endpoints. A 407 or other non-2xx CONNECT answer fails with an error that never contains the credentials; proxy credentials and URLs are redacted in logs. Unit group `proxy_` (configuration parsing, `NO_PROXY` matching, CONNECT request bytes, response handling, redaction).

An Aspire `test-proxy` resource (test-only .NET CONNECT proxy with a tunnel counter, optional required credentials and a deny list) proves: plaintext and TLS endpoints over all three transports connect through the proxy (counter increases, the service sees the proxy as the peer); wrong credentials fail with the 407 error; a `NO_PROXY` match bypasses the proxy. Scenario `proxy` on native and Android, and on iOS in CI.

requirements.title: Suspension-aware liveness
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Recover promptly when the OS suspends or freezes the app, instead of waiting for timers that fired late.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: The shared liveness scheduler detects suspension on both targets: when a liveness wake happens more than one keep-alive interval after its scheduled deadline, measured with a sleep-inclusive clock (wall clock or boot time) as the .NET client's `DateTime.UtcNow` checks are, so device sleep counts, the client sends a Ping at once; when the elapsed silence has reached the server timeout, the connection ends immediately with the server-timeout error, as the .NET client's `OnServerTimeout` (the reconnection policy runs; a server timeout is not resumed, stateful or not), rather than after a further server timeout. Detection never fires during normal operation (no false positives at the default intervals). Unit group `suspension_` with an injected clock.

Scenario `suspend-resume`: the runner suspends the scenario process each time the scenario signals readiness, for the duration the readiness line names, then resumes it: native on Windows (`NtSuspendProcess`/`NtResumeProcess`) and Unix (`SIGSTOP`/`SIGCONT`), Android (`kill -STOP`/`-CONT` on the device process), iOS (the simulator process is a host process), Chromium (the page's JavaScript stopped and restarted through CDP `Debugger.pause`/`Debugger.resume`: no timers or events run while the clock advances, as in a frozen page). A stateful and an ordinary client (both with a reconnection policy) each have an invocation pending. First suspension, 20 s (longer than the 15 s keep-alive interval, shorter than the service's 30 s client timeout): both clients keep their connections (same connection ids, no lifecycle events) and their pending invocations complete. Second suspension, 40 s (longer than the client timeout; ASP.NET Core then ends the hub connection, `HubConnectionContext.CheckClientTimeout` calling `AbortAllowReconnect`, so no client can resume it): within 5 s of resuming, both clients have detected the loss, their pending invocations have failed with a connection error, and they have reconnected on new connections. Firefox and WebKit are catalog exclusions (Playwright offers CDP only for Chromium), recorded with the reason.

The documentation (`docs/06-connection-lifecycle.md`, `docs/09-platforms.md`) covers app lifecycle integration for iOS (`pause()` on entering the background, `resume()` on becoming active), Android (`onStop`/`onStart`) and browsers (`visibilitychange`, page freeze), and what suspension detection does when an app does not pause.

requirements.title: TLS provider and Android platform-verifier proof
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Prove the alternative crypto provider and the Android platform verifier at runtime.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: `RAYX_SIGNALR_E2E_TLS_PROVIDER=aws-lc-rs` makes the runners build the e2e binaries with `--no-default-features --features messagepack,tls-platform-verifier,tls-aws-lc-rs` (Android adds `tls-webpki-roots`); the TLS-dependent scenarios (`tls`, `connect-negotiate`, `negotiate-redirect`, and `proxy`, which covers TLS over all three transports) pass with it on native and Android, and on iOS in CI.

A test-only Android app (`tests/android-app`, Gradle with Kotlin, minSdk 24) embeds a `cdylib` harness (`tests/android-harness`) that reuses the `tests/e2e` scenarios (through the `tests/e2e-scenarios` library crate, which compiles the same sources) through a JNI `runScenario(name, protocol, environment)` entry. It initializes the platform verifier with `rayx_signalr::tls::android::init_with_env(env, context)` from the instrumentation `Context`, and the platform verifier trusts the per-run test CA through the Android trust store, without extra PEM roots: the app, made device owner on the emulator by the runner, installs the CA as a user CA (`DevicePolicyManager.installCaCert`) for each scenario and removes it, and the runner removes the device owner and the app after the run. (rustls-platform-verifier's Android component initializes its `TrustManagerFactory` with the `AndroidCAStore` keystore, so it trusts system and user CAs and does not read the app's network security config.) New targets `android-app` (debug APK) and `android-app-release` (minified release APK with the documented ProGuard keep rule) run `tls` (platform-verifier trust and rejection of an untrusted second CA), `connect-negotiate` and `invoke` on the emulator through `am instrument`, with the same bounds and diagnostics as other cells.

The Android documentation (`docs/09-platforms.md`) matches the working test app (the Gradle repository and version wiring, the ProGuard rule and the initialization call are copied from it), and the limitations chapter (`docs/12-limitations.md`) no longer lists the Android platform verifier or `aws-lc-rs` as unproven, and states which CAs the Android platform verifier trusts (system and user CAs, not the app's network security config).

requirements.title: CI, documentation and completion
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Run everything in CI and document the finished client.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: Workflows run every new dimension through Aspire: the e2e jobs select `RAYX_SIGNALR_E2E_TRANSPORTS=all`; `e2e / android-app` (emulator runner, debug and release APKs); `e2e / tls-aws-lc (<target>)` for native (ubuntu, windows, macos), Android and iOS; `e2e / soak` on `schedule` (nightly) and `workflow_dispatch` with 900 s; `perf / compare` on `workflow_dispatch` and `schedule` with `RAYX_SIGNALR_PERF_SCALE=full`, uploading `artifacts-temp/perf` as an artifact (not failure-only, 30-day retention, still no secrets). The typed-error scenario runs in every e2e job; delivered stretch features run too: SOCKS5 and PAC scenarios with the proxy scenarios, `e2e / os-proxy (windows, macos)` on ephemeral runners with `RAYX_SIGNALR_E2E_ALLOW_SYSTEM_CHANGES=1`, HTTP/2 scenarios in the native and Android jobs, and HTTP/3 scenarios on ubuntu (with `libmsquic`) and windows. `WorkflowContract` asserts every new job, its platform and its selection inside its own job block and keeps the existing governance (least privilege, no publishing, pinned actions).

A GitHub Actions run of every workflow on the epic branch is green, including all transports on every e2e target, `e2e / android-app`, the aws-lc-rs jobs, a dispatched `e2e / soak` (900 s) and a dispatched `perf / compare` whose report meets R2.C4; the run URLs are recorded in the final review.

The documentation (`docs/` chapters, README overview) covers error handling (the `Error`/`ErrorKind` model and the migration from `String` errors), transports and fallback, proxies (including the delivered SOCKS5, PAC and OS-settings support), HTTP versions (delivered HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 support and what browsers do), the access-token factory, browser authentication, `with_connect_timeout`, suspension handling and the measured performance (the `perf / compare` report summary with its environment); the limitations chapter (`docs/12-limitations.md`) lists only the residual risks that remain (with the proven ones removed); the testing chapter (`docs/14-testing.md`) and, if it still exists, the RayX.SignalR skill's validation list name the new categories and selectors; memory records the new behavior and decisions.

requirements.title: Typed error model (mandatory)
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Replace `String` errors in the public API with one structured, matchable error type on both targets.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: `rayx_signalr::Error` (`#[non_exhaustive]`, `Clone + Send + Sync + 'static`, `std::error::Error` with `source()` chains through `Arc`) and the `Copy` `ErrorKind` returned by `Error::kind()` cover at least: `Configuration` (rejected before I/O, naming the setting), `Negotiate` (HTTP status and a bounded, redacted body excerpt), `Authentication` (401/403 status, or the access-token factory's failure as the source), `Timeout` (which operation - connect, negotiate, handshake, server timeout - and the bound), `Tls`, `Proxy`, `Transport` (which transport, and whether the server allowed reconnecting), `TransportUnavailable` (every attempted transport with its error), `Handshake`, `Protocol` (malformed or unexpected frames), `Serialization` (a payload could not be encoded or decoded into the requested type), `Hub` (the server's invocation or stream error message), `ConnectionClosed` (local disconnect, server close with its optional message, or reconnect attempts exhausted), `Paused` and `Canceled`. Helpers: `Error::status()`, `Error::is_transient()` (true for timeouts, dropped transports, 5xx and 408/429 negotiate answers). `Display` is stable, human-readable and redacted (no tokens, credentials, proxy userinfo or `access_token` values). Unit group `error_model_` covers construction, classification, `Display` redaction, `source()` chains and `is_transient`.

Every public fallible API on both targets uses the typed model: `connect`/`connect_with`, `invoke*`, `send*`, stream errors (`error()` returns `Option<&Error>`), `pause`/`resume`, configuration validation, disconnection/reconnection handler information (the reason the connection dropped), and the TLS/Android initialization functions. No public signature contains a `String` error. `tests/public_error_types.rs` asserts the signatures at compile time (function-pointer and trait-bound assertions for every public fallible item), and the wasm build compiles the same public surface.

E2e scenario `error-kinds` on every target asserts the kind and structured fields of: a hub method that throws (`Hub` with the server message), an unauthenticated connect (`Authentication`, 401), an unknown hub path (`Negotiate`, 404), the hanging negotiate with a 2 s bound (`Timeout` naming negotiate), a payload that cannot be deserialized into the requested type (`Serialization`), invoking after `disconnect` (`ConnectionClosed`), invoking while paused (`Paused`), a server close with an error message (`ConnectionClosed` carrying it), and natively an untrusted certificate (`Tls`); no `Display` output contains the test token. Existing scenarios and unit tests that matched error strings are migrated to kinds in the same sprint.

The documentation (`docs/` chapters, README overview) covers error handling with matching examples and a migration section from `String` errors; `Cargo.toml` moves to the next major version; the documentation of every public fallible item names its error kinds.

requirements.title: SOCKS5, proxy auto-config and OS proxy settings (mandatory since 2026-10-07)
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Extend native proxy support beyond HTTP CONNECT, if feasible (see the stretch rule in the scope).

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: `with_proxy` and the proxy environment variables accept SOCKS proxy URLs as the official .NET client (`SocksHelper`, `HttpEnvironmentProxy`) does: `socks5://` and `socks5h://` (both send domain names to the proxy, which resolves them; IP literals go as IPv4/IPv6 addresses), `socks4://` (resolved locally to IPv4) and `socks4a://` (proxy-side DNS), default port 1080, with optional username/password authentication (RFC 1929 for SOCKS5, the user id for SOCKS4). Every native connection (negotiate and all transports) tunnels through SOCKS with TLS inside the tunnel; failures are `ErrorKind::Proxy` naming the SOCKS reply code and never contain credentials. Unit group `socks_` (handshake bytes, auth, address types, reply codes, truncated replies, SOCKS4/4a); scenario `proxy-socks` (the Aspire test proxy gains a SOCKS5 listener with a counter and required credentials) on native and Android.

Behind the non-default `proxy-pac` feature (pure-Rust JavaScript engine, no C toolchain), `with_proxy_auto_config(url)` loads a PAC script (`http`, `https` or `file`) once per connect under the connect timeout, evaluates `FindProxyForURL(url, host)` with the standard helper functions (`isPlainHostName`, `dnsDomainIs`, `localHostOrDomainIs`, `isResolvable`, `isInNet`, `dnsResolve`, `myIpAddress`, `dnsDomainLevels`, `shExpMatch`, `weekdayRange`, `dateRange`, `timeRange`) under a bounded evaluation time, and tries the returned `PROXY`/`HTTPS`/`SOCKS`/`SOCKS5`/`DIRECT` entries in order. Script load or evaluation failures are `ErrorKind::Proxy`. Unit group `pac_`; scenario `proxy-pac` (the test proxy serves PAC scripts that select HTTP, SOCKS5 and DIRECT per host) on native and Android.

The default proxy resolution (also selectable with `with_os_proxy()`) resolves the proxy per URL from the operating system, as the .NET client's default proxy does: Windows through WinHTTP (current-user settings including auto-detect and PAC), macOS and iOS through CFNetwork (system settings including PAC), Android through `java.net.ProxySelector` via JNI (initialized with the same Android initialization as the platform verifier), and Linux through the proxy environment variables. Unit group `os_proxy_` with injected platform readers; scenario `os-proxy` on `android-app` (emulator global proxy set and restored by the runner) and, in CI only, on ephemeral Windows and macOS runners that opt in to system changes.

`with_proxy` and the proxy environment variables accept `https://` proxy URLs, as the .NET client (since .NET 8) does: the client runs TLS to the proxy with the connection's own TLS configuration (trust roots, the explicit rustls provider, never an accept-all verifier), sends the `CONNECT` request with the same 407/Basic challenge flow as `http://` proxies inside that TLS session, and runs the endpoint's own TLS inside the tunnel for secure endpoints. A proxy certificate that does not verify fails with `ErrorKind::Proxy` naming the proxy (never the credentials). Unit group `https_proxy_`; scenario `proxy-https` (the Aspire test proxy gains a TLS listener with the run's test certificate, a counter and required credentials) on native and Android.

requirements.title: HTTP/2 (mandatory since 2026-10-07)
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Use HTTP/2 natively where the server supports it, if feasible.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: Native `with_http_version(HttpVersion)`: `Http1`, `Auto` (default, as in the .NET client: TLS offers ALPN `h2, http/1.1` and uses HTTP/2 for negotiate, Long Polling and Server-Sent Events when negotiated; plaintext stays HTTP/1.1; WebSockets stay HTTP/1.1) and `Http2` (HTTP/2 only; plaintext uses h2c prior knowledge; fails with `ErrorKind::Transport` when unavailable). Over HTTP/2, negotiate, Long Polling and Server-Sent Events of one connect attempt share one multiplexed connection (each start and reconnect attempt opens new ones, as a new .NET `HttpConnection`; a request the server never processed is sent once more on a new connection, any other is never repeated), and with `Http2`, WebSockets use RFC 8441 extended CONNECT (an error when the server does not enable it). As the .NET client turns HTTP/2 off when credentials are configured (`Http2HttpMessageHandler` only without `UseDefaultCredentials`/`Credentials`), integrated Windows authentication keeps every request on HTTP/1.1 whatever the configured version, as .NET lowers `Http2` with credentials instead of failing. Works inside CONNECT and SOCKS5 tunnels. Unit group `http2_`.

The test service gains an HTTPS endpoint with HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 and an h2c endpoint, and records each request's protocol. Scenario `http2` proves negotiate and all three transports over HTTP/2 (WebSockets through extended CONNECT) for JSON and MessagePack (Server-Sent Events JSON only), plus `Auto` falling back to HTTP/1.1 against an HTTP/1.1-only endpoint, on native and Android.

requirements.title: HTTP/3 (stretch)
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Offer HTTP/3 natively as an experimental option, if feasible.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: Behind the non-default `http3` feature (QUIC with the connection's own rustls configuration and explicit provider), `HttpVersion::Http3` carries negotiate, Long Polling and Server-Sent Events over HTTP/3, and WebSockets over RFC 9220 only if the server supports it (verified first; otherwise WebSockets is unavailable over HTTP/3 and transport selection skips it with a recorded reason). `HttpVersion::Http3Preferred` falls back to TCP (HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1) within the connect timeout when QUIC cannot be established (for example UDP blocked). Unit group `http3_`.

The test service gains a Kestrel HTTP/3 endpoint (where the host supports it) and records the request protocol. Scenario `http3` proves negotiate and the available transports over HTTP/3, and `Http3Preferred` falling back to TCP against an endpoint without HTTP/3, on native (Windows 11 and Linux with `libmsquic`) and Android; macOS and iOS hosts are catalog exclusions with the recorded Kestrel limitation.

requirements.title: Parity with the official .NET client (mandatory)
requirements.descriptionMarkdown: Match the observable behavior of the official .NET SignalR client wherever this client differs, so applications and servers see the same semantics from either client.

criteria.descriptionMarkdown: `SignalRClient::disconnect(&self)` stops the connection for every handle, as `HubConnection.StopAsync` does: clones, registered callbacks and live `InvocationContext`s do not keep it open; pending invocations and open streams of every handle end at once with `ConnectionClosed` (`CloseReason::Local`); later calls, `pause` and `resume` on any handle fail with the same error; every handle reports `Closed`; a running reconnect or pause is superseded; and the hub sees exactly one disconnect. `disconnect`, `register` and `unregister` called from inside a registered callback return (no storage lock is held while callbacks run), and a server-triggered callback can disconnect its own connection. Dropping a handle still closes the connection only when it is the last one. Unit group `disconnect_` and e2e scenario `disconnect-every-handle` on every target; `concurrency-and-clones` proves that dropping a clone keeps the connection for the others.

An unstarted client, as `HubConnectionBuilder.Build()` gives: `SignalRClient::new(domain, hub, configure)` validates the configuration and builds a client without I/O; `register`, the lifecycle hooks of R16.C4 and handlers work before `start().await`, which negotiates and connects (`connect_with` becomes `new` plus `start`). Hub messages sent from `OnConnectedAsync` reach callbacks registered before `start`. Unit group `client_start_`; scenario `connected-callback` (a test hub whose `OnConnectedAsync` sends to the caller) on every target.

Restart after stop, as `StartAsync` after `StopAsync`: `start().await` on a client stopped by `disconnect` or ended remotely runs a fresh negotiate (new connection id) and keeps registered callbacks and hooks; `start` on a client that is connecting, connected, reconnecting or paused fails without changing it; `disconnect` during `start` or a reconnect cancels it. Registered callbacks and hooks never keep a client alive (the registry holds it weakly; `SignalRClient::downgrade` gives applications the same `WeakSignalRClient`), so dropping the last handle stops a started client and a failed start never leaks it. Unit group `client_restart_`; scenario `restart-after-stop` on every target.

Lifecycle hooks matching the .NET `Closed`, `Reconnecting` and `Reconnected` events: `on_closed(Fn(Option<&Error>))`, `on_reconnecting(Fn(&Error))` and `on_reconnected(Fn(Option<&str>))`, several per event, registrable before `start`, alongside automatic reconnect. After a drop: pending ordinary work fails, then `Reconnecting(reason)` (not raised when the policy allows no attempt), then `Reconnected(new connection id)` or `Closed(error)`; `Closed(None)` after `disconnect`, or `Closed` with an `ErrorKind::Canceled` error when the stop interrupted a reconnect (as .NET's `OperationCanceledException`). Events keep that order whatever runs concurrently (natively they are raised under the connection's state lock, and a run's `Reconnected` while its connection installs). Hooks never block the connection (natively they run on the Tokio blocking pool); native hook panics are caught and logged. Unit group `lifecycle_events_`; scenario `lifecycle-events` on every target.

`connection_id()` returns the negotiated connection id (`Context.ConnectionId` on the hub), as `HubConnection.ConnectionId`: a new id after every fresh connection, unchanged after a stateful resume, `None` with `skip_negotiation` and while not connected. Unit group `connection_id_`; scenario `connection-id` on every target.

Client results behave as in the .NET client: a result-expecting invocation (one with an invocation id) for a target without a callback gets the error Completion `Client didn't provide a result.`; `InvocationContext::fail(message)` sends an error Completion; a context dropped without completing sends the missing-result error; a second `complete` or `fail` returns an error locally and sends nothing; the answer goes to the logical connection the call arrived on (kept by a stateful resume; after an ordinary reconnect or a fresh negotiation, answering fails locally with `ErrorKind::Transport`). Unit group `client_results_`; scenario `client-result-errors` (the test service records the `HubException` text its `InvokeAsync` observed) on every target.

Several callbacks per target run in registration order, as `HubConnection.On` handlers do; each `CallbackHandler::unregister` removes only its own callback and `remove(target)` removes them all. Unit group `callback_registry_`.

Server-to-client calls are dispatched on a per-connection task in arrival order and never under a storage lock, as the .NET client's separate dispatch loop does: completions, stream items, Pings and Acks never wait on a callback; asynchronous callbacks (`register_async`) are awaited one at a time, except that a call expecting a result starts in arrival order and continues on its own task once a callback waits, so it never holds later calls (as `HubConnection`'s receive loop does not await result-expecting dispatches); natively a panicking callback (sync, typed, or an asynchronous callback's factory or future) is caught and logged and the connection keeps working, and an unanswered result-expecting call is answered with the panic message as the .NET client answers with a throwing handler's exception message; `register`, `unregister` and `disconnect` inside a callback return. Unit group `callback_dispatch_`; scenario `callback-dispatch` (a slow callback does not delay an invoke completion) on every target. Natively registered callbacks are `Send + Sync` (they may run on any thread of the connection's runtime), so no lock is held while one runs.

Typed callbacks (`register_typed` with a tuple of argument types) decode the arguments before the callback runs; on a count or type mismatch the callback is not called, the failure is logged, and a result-expecting invocation gets the .NET binding-failure Completion. Unit group `callback_binding_` for JSON and MessagePack.

MessagePack callback arguments decode from the original MessagePack values, as the .NET binder does (binary data, timestamps and non-string map keys survive), instead of through JSON values. Unit group `callback_msgpack_args_`; scenario `msgpack-fidelity` (a callback carrying `byte[]`, `DateTime` and `Dictionary<int,string>`) on every target, MessagePack only.
`invoke::<()>` accepts and discards any result, as the non-generic `InvokeAsync` does. Unit group `void_invoke_` for JSON and MessagePack completions with results.

Pending invocations and callbacks live in separate namespaces and invocation ids are per-connection counters (`"1"`, `"2"`, ...) as in the .NET client, so a callback target never collides with an invocation id. Unit group `invocation_ids_`.

A Ping is sent right after every successful handshake (connect and ordinary reconnect, not after a stateful resume), as the .NET client does, so ASP.NET Core arms its client timeout. Unit group `liveness_initial_ping_` against a loopback WebSocket peer for both protocols.

Stopping is graceful as in `StopAsync`: a SignalR Close message (`{"type":7}` or `[7,nil,false]`) is sent before the transport closes, and the asynchronous `stop().await` completes when the transport has closed or after `with_close_timeout` (default 5 s); `disconnect()` stays the synchronous form, and its background close (also on the last handle's drop) is bounded by the same timeout. The hub counts the client's Close message (a protocol wrapper in the test service) and its `OnDisconnectedAsync` sees no exception. Unit group `graceful_stop_`; scenario `graceful-stop` on every target.

Stateful reconnect behaves as in the .NET client: after an ungraceful transport loss the client makes exactly one immediate resume to the same connection, independent of the reconnection policy, keeping status `Connected`, raising no events and buffering sends for resend; when that resume fails, or after a server Close or a graceful close, the connection ends and the policy reconnects with a fresh negotiate (new connection id). Unit group `stateful_transparent_`; scenarios `stateful-transparent-resume` and `stateful-resume-fallback` on native, Chromium and Android.

Stateful Acks go out at most once per second and only when something new arrived (plus one after quiescence), and a message larger than the buffer limit is still sent with backpressure applying to the next send, as the .NET `MessageBuffer` does. Unit group `stateful_ack_cadence_` with an injected clock.

A malformed or unexpected message ends the transport with `ErrorKind::Protocol` and the reconnection policy runs (a stateful protocol violation reconnects with a fresh negotiate), as in the .NET client; unknown new message types are ignored. Unit group `protocol_violation_`.

Native WebSocket requests carry the bearer token only in the `Authorization` header, never as `access_token` in the URL (also with `skip_negotiation`), as the .NET client outside browsers does; browsers keep `access_token`. Unit group `token_placement_`; the `request-headers` scenario asserts that the native WebSocket URL carries no token.

Every native HTTP request and WebSocket upgrade sends `User-Agent` in the official client's format with a rayx product token and `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest`; negotiate also sends `Accept: */*`; browsers send `X-SignalR-User-Agent`. Unit group `request_headers_`; scenario `request-headers` (the test service echoes request headers) on every target.

`with_header(name, value)` adds a header to negotiate, the native WebSocket upgrade and the HTTP transports, as `HttpConnectionOptions.Headers` does (browsers: negotiate and HTTP transports, with a warning for the WebSocket); invalid names or values fail `connect` before I/O with `ErrorKind::Configuration`. Covered by `request_headers_` and the `request-headers` scenario.

A native per-client cookie jar (optionally supplied by the application) stores negotiate `Set-Cookie` headers and sends matching cookies on the WebSocket upgrade, the HTTP transports and reconnects, as the .NET client's `CookieContainer` does (browsers manage cookies themselves). Unit group `cookie_jar_`; scenario `cookies` (the test service sets an affinity cookie on negotiate and rejects upgrades without it) on native and Android.

A negotiate response without `negotiateVersion` is treated as version 0 (connect with `id` set to the connection id), and a classic ASP.NET SignalR response yields a specific error, as in the .NET client. Unit group `negotiate_parity_`.
`skip_negotiation()` together with stateful reconnect connects without stateful reconnect and logs a warning, as the .NET client does, instead of failing. Covered by `negotiate_parity_`.

Client-to-server streaming as in the .NET client: `ArgumentConfiguration::stream(impl Stream<Item = T>)` sends the stream id in `streamIds`, the items as StreamItem messages and a final Completion (with the .NET texts for a client error or cancellation); nothing is sent after the connection ends and upload streams are canceled on close; works with `invoke`, `send` and `enumerate`. Unit group `client_streams_`; scenario `client-to-server-stream` (hub parameters `IAsyncEnumerable<int>` and `ChannelReader<int>`) on every target.

Reconnection policies receive a `RetryContext` (`previous_retry_count`, `elapsed`, `retry_reason: Error`) as `IRetryPolicy.NextRetryDelay` does (the existing `next_retry_delay(count, elapsed)` keeps working through a default method); a panicking policy stops reconnecting; a delay-list policy matches `WithAutomaticReconnect(TimeSpan[])`. Unit group `retry_context_`.

A call made while a reconnect attempt is in flight waits for that attempt and then runs on the new connection or fails with the attempt's error, as the .NET client's connection lock does; during the policy delay calls fail at once. Calls during a start wait the same way. Unit group `reconnect_call_wait_` (start and reconnect attempts, success and failure, on a loopback test server); scenario `reconnect-call-wait` on every target (the test service holds the attempt's negotiate request).

`with_client_certificate(chain_pem, key_pem)` presents a client certificate on negotiate, WebSocket and HTTP-transport TLS natively, as `HttpConnectionOptions.ClientCertificates` does (browsers use their own certificate store). Unit group `client_certificates_`; scenario `client-certificate` (a Kestrel endpoint requiring client certificates) on native and Android.

Integrated Windows authentication as `UseDefaultCredentials` and `Credentials`: `with_default_credentials()` (the current account) and `with_credentials(user, password, domain)` authenticate negotiate, the WebSocket upgrade and the HTTP transports with HTTP Negotiate and NTLM (Kerberos where available). Unit group `integrated_auth_` (challenge and response handling with an injected security provider); scenario `windows-auth` (a test hub behind ASP.NET Core Negotiate authentication) on native Windows; other targets are catalog exclusions with the recorded reason (no Kerberos realm on Linux and macOS hosts; browsers authenticate natively).

Transport hooks as `HttpMessageHandlerFactory` and `WebSocketConfiguration`: `with_request_hook` adjusts every native HTTP request and the WebSocket upgrade (browsers: negotiate and HTTP-transport requests), and `with_tls_config_hook` adjusts the rustls `ClientConfig` before use. Unit group `transport_hooks_`; the `request-headers` scenario includes a hook-added header.

Liveness durations are accepted as the .NET client accepts them (no `connect` failure for zero values or a server timeout not above the keep-alive interval), and values that cannot work are logged as warnings. Unit group `liveness_parity_`.

An optional invocation-header hook adds headers (for example W3C `traceparent`) to Invocation and StreamInvocation messages in both protocols, as the .NET client does with an Activity listener. Unit group `invocation_headers_` with golden frames.

Inbound framing carries partial JSON records and MessagePack messages across WebSocket messages, as the .NET client's pipe-based parser does, and there is no fixed message-size cap (`with_maximum_message_size`, unbounded by default). Unit group `framing_carryover_`.

JSON payloads (results, stream items, callback arguments) that do not decode with the application's exact Serde names are decoded again matching field names case-insensitively, as System.Text.Json's web defaults read (user decision 2026-10-07); outbound names stay the application's. Unit group `case_insensitive_payload_`.

`Error::server_message()` returns the server's hub or Close error text verbatim, as `HubException.Message` does (user decision 2026-10-07), while `Display` stays redacted per R12.C1. Unit group `server_text_`.
